title: Blessed, and More Than the Law Asked
sum: Jesus sees the crowds, climbs a mountain and sits down to teach his disciples, with the crowds listening (5:1–2). The Sermon on the Mount, the first of five long speeches in Matthew, runs to the end of chapter 7. It opens with eight blessings on unlikely people: the poor in spirit, mourners, the gentle, the hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, peacemakers and the persecuted (5:3–12). The disciples are the salt of the earth and the light of the world (5:13–16).

Then Jesus states his program: he has come not to do away with the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them, and his followers' righteousness must go far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees (5:17–20). Six times he quotes what was said long ago and adds, "But I myself tell you": anger as well as murder, lust as well as adultery, divorce, oaths, revenge and love for enemies (5:21–47). The chapter ends with the call to be perfect, as the heavenly Father is perfect (5:48).
readings: Read as the charter of the kingdom

The Beatitudes announce who belongs to God's coming kingdom, and the six sayings show what life in it looks like. On this reading the chapter describes a real way of life for Jesus' followers now, hard but possible with God's help, and the sermon's audience is every disciple.
Read as Torah from the mountain

Jesus goes up a mountain like Moses and teaches on the commandments, but he speaks in his own name. On this reading the chapter is about Jesus' authority over the Law: he keeps every iota of it while showing its deepest intent, and he places himself where Moses' voice stood.

Who can avoid all anger, all lust, every careless word? Many readers, especially Lutherans, have read the chapter as showing how far everyone falls short, so that they turn to God's mercy. Others answer that Jesus expects to be obeyed (7:24–27) and that the sermon assumes grace from its first word, "Blessed."

views.H: The setting is the hill country west of the Sea of Galilee, under Herod Antipas, where farmers, fishermen and laborers lived with debt, taxes and Roman soldiers who could force them to carry gear (5:41). The examples are local: the Temple altar (5:23), the Sanhedrin (5:22), the certificate of divorce (5:31), oaths by Jerusalem (5:35). Many historians think the sermon gathers sayings Jesus spoke on many occasions; most agree that the core sayings, love for enemies, no oaths, no divorce, go back to Jesus himself.
views.C: Most critical scholars think Matthew built the sermon from Mark, from sayings he shared with Luke (the source often called Q, whose sermon is Luke 6:20–49), and from his own material (the antitheses on murder, adultery and oaths, the teaching on secret piety). Luke's shorter Sermon on the Plain has four blessings and four woes. Hans Dieter Betz argued that 5:3–7:27 was an earlier Jewish-Christian summary of Jesus' teaching that Matthew took over whole; most scholars think Matthew shaped it himself.
views.L: The first of Matthew's five discourses, framed by the mountain (5:1; 8:1) and the closing formula (7:28). The main body runs from "the Law or the Prophets" (5:17) to "That is the Law and the Prophets" (7:12). The Beatitudes come in two sets of four, each ending with righteousness; the antitheses come in two sets of three, the second set opening with "Again" (5:33). Jesus on the mountain as a new Moses (2:13–21; 4:2) gives a new teaching on the Law.
views.J: Almost every line has Jewish parallels: Psalm 37 behind 5:5, Isaiah 61 behind 5:3–4, Pharisaic debates on divorce and oaths, the rabbinic "fence around the Torah." Jewish scholars such as David Flusser and Amy-Jill Levine read the antitheses as an intensifying of the Law within Judaism, not a break with it. The sermon was later used to set a "Christian ethic of love" against a "Jewish ethic of law," a contrast that misreads both the sermon and Judaism; 5:43 in particular has been misused that way.
views.T: The church fathers quoted this chapter more than any other passage of the Gospels. Augustine's The Lord's Sermon on the Mount and Chrysostom's homilies read it as the perfect pattern of Christian life. Medieval theology distinguished precepts for all from counsels of perfection for monks and nuns; the Reformers rejected that split; the Anabaptists took 5:33–42 literally and refused oaths and the sword. In the liturgy the Beatitudes are sung in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy and read on All Saints' Day in the West.

deep.b: The Greek is the SBL Greek New Testament, checked word by word against the STEPBible TAGNT, which marks where NA28, the Tyndale House edition, Westcott and Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Robinson-Pierpont Byzantine text differ. Manuscript evidence for the variants was taken from Metzger's Textual Commentary and from the apparatus of Tischendorf's eighth edition, read page by page for Matthew 5–7 in the Source Library scan. The papyri and the Editio Critica Maior were not consulted directly; Matthew has no Editio Critica Maior yet.

deep.h: The six "But I myself tell you" sayings
deep.b:
Each saying quotes the Law or a common understanding of it, then gives Jesus' word:

  • Murder (5:21–26): not only murder but contempt and anger, with two examples of making peace.
  • Adultery (5:27–30): not only the act but the look that wants another man's wife.
  • Divorce (5:31–32): not a certificate that makes it proper, but no divorce except for sexual sin.
  • Oaths (5:33–37): not only true oaths, but no oaths, because all speech is before God.
  • Revenge (5:38–42): not limited payback, but no payback, and generosity to the one who takes.
  • Love (5:43–47): not love for the neighbor only, but love and prayer for the enemy.

The first two go deeper than the command; the next four go beyond what the Law permitted. None asks anyone to do what the Law forbids, and Jesus never says the Law was wrong. Christians have long argued whether these are new commands that replace Moses (an older Protestant and Catholic view), the true meaning that Moses intended (Calvin and most Reformed), or kingdom ideals for a future age (classic dispensationalism). Jewish readers have often noted that rabbis made similar moves: the Talmud compares anger to idolatry (Shabbat 105b) and shaming someone in public to shedding blood (Bava Metzia 58b).

Under the Law only a husband could divorce, by writing a certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). The schools of Shammai and Hillel, a generation before Jesus, argued over the grounds in Deuteronomy 24:1, "something indecent": Shammai said only sexual unfaithfulness; Hillel said any cause, "even if she spoiled his dish"; Rabbi Akiba later added, "even if he found another more beautiful" (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). The Pharisees' question in 19:3, "for any cause?", uses the Hillelite phrase. The Damascus Document from the Qumran movement criticized men who took "two wives in their lifetime" (Damascus Document 4:20–5:2). Roman law let either spouse end a marriage easily.

Jesus' teaching was stricter than any of these. Mark, Luke and Paul give it without exception; Matthew includes "except for sexual sin" both here and at 19:9. Many scholars think Matthew made explicit an exception that Jewish hearers would assume, since the Law required (or strongly expected) a man to divorce an adulterous wife. Others think the exception concerns marriages forbidden by Leviticus 18. The oldest church reading, from Jerome and Augustine, is that it allows separation but not remarriage. The churches' answers differ; see the card below.

deep.h: Turn the other cheek: four ways of reading
deep.b:
1. Personal, not public. Augustine and Luther taught that Christians must not seek revenge for wrongs done to themselves, but that rulers, judges and soldiers may and must restrain evil (Romans 13:1–7). Luther called this the distinction between the person and the office.

2. For all believers, literally. The Anabaptists (Schleitheim, 1527), later the Quakers and the historic peace churches, held that Jesus' followers may not use the sword at all, in war or as magistrates.

3. Creative nonviolence. Walter Wink argued that each example is a way to resist with dignity: turning the other cheek forces a backhanded attacker to strike as an equal; giving up the robe in court leaves the creditor facing a naked debtor and his own shame; going a second mile puts the soldier in breach of rules. Many scholars find this too clever. Wink built on the practice of Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., and his reading has influenced later nonviolent movements.

4. Kingdom ethic. Classic dispensationalists read these commands as the law of the future kingdom, to be fully obeyed only when Christ reigns.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Beatitudes as a portrait of Jesus
deep.b: Read after the whole Gospel, each Beatitude describes Jesus himself in Matthew's story: he is "gentle" (11:29; 21:5), mourns over Jerusalem (23:37), is "merciful" to those who cry out (9:27; 20:30–34), fulfills all righteousness (3:15), is reviled, persecuted and lied about "on account of" his claims (26:59–68), and is called Son of God at the cross (27:54), which matches the peacemakers' title in 5:9. If this is deliberate, the Beatitudes are not only a list of virtues but a sketch of the one who speaks them, and the disciples are blessed as they come to share his life. This reading overlaps with Dale Allison's observation that Matthew's ethics follow the pattern of Jesus' own life (The Sermon on the Mount, 1999); the link to each Beatitude is my suggestion.

echoes: Luke 6:20–49; Exodus 19:3; Exodus 20:13–14; Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 19:12; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 18:13; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Psalm 24:3–4; Psalm 37:11; Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 61:1–3; Isaiah 66:1; 19:3–12; 22:34–40; 23:16–22; Romans 12:14–21; James 5:12; 1 Peter 2:21–23

settings.by: Jesus, seated on a mountain in Galilee as a teacher
settings.to: his disciples, who come to him (5:1), with the crowds from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan listening around them (4:25; 7:28)
settings.when: early in Jesus' work in Galilee, after he has called his first disciples and his fame has spread through healing (4:18–25)
settings.why: To show the disciples what life looks like when God reigns: who is blessed, how the Law is to be kept from the heart, how to pray and give and fast for God alone, how to trust the Father, and how to build a life that will stand at the judgment. Because the crowds overhear, it is also an invitation: this is what following Jesus means.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, read it as the teaching their Lord left them for living as a faithful Jewish community distinct from the synagogue, and as the core of what the risen Jesus told them to teach the nations (28:20).
views: Many readers stress 5:1: the sermon is instruction for those already following Jesus, not a way to earn entry.
Others stress 7:28: the crowds hear too, and the sermon calls all Israel to the kingdom.

Luke sets a shorter sermon on a level place after the choosing of the Twelve (Luke 6:12–20), spoken to disciples with a great crowd present. Most scholars think both evangelists arranged sayings Jesus spoke on many occasions.

settings.to: the disciples, with the crowds listening; in 5:11–12 directly "you," the disciples
settings.when: at the opening of the sermon
settings.why: To announce that God's kingdom belongs to people the world counts as losers: the poor, the grieving, the meek, the persecuted. For disciples who had left boats and families (4:18–22), the blessings promised that God sees them and that their reward is great. Knowing the hearers were poor Galileans, some already facing hostility, keeps the blessings from becoming mere ideals.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, heard 5:10–12 as words about their own persecution (10:17–23; 23:34).
views: The Beatitudes announce grace: God blesses those who have nothing.
They describe virtues the disciples are to grow into, a ladder of character (Augustine, Chrysostom).

settings.when: right after the blessings on the persecuted
settings.why: To tell a small, persecuted group that they have a public calling: to season and preserve the world and to light it, as Israel was called to be a light to the nations. They must not hide or lose their distinctiveness to avoid trouble.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, were tempted, under pressure, either to withdraw from public life or to blend in.

settings.what: Jesus on the Law and the Prophets
settings.to: the disciples, and any listener who suspected that Jesus was setting the Law aside
settings.when: before the six sayings on the Law, as their heading
settings.why: To answer a charge before it is made: Jesus does not abolish the Torah. Every detail stands, and his followers must keep it with a righteousness deeper than that of the respected teachers. The sayings that follow must be read in that light.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, were arguing with synagogue leaders, and perhaps with other Christians, about whether followers of Jesus still kept the Law. This passage answered: yes, as Jesus taught it.
views: Many critical scholars think Matthew's church kept the Law, including food and Sabbath laws, and that 5:19 opposes Christians who taught otherwise.
Most Christian interpreters read "fulfill" so that the Law continues as Jesus interprets it, and some parts are fulfilled and no longer binding in their old form.

settings.to: the disciples, addressed as fellow members of a community of "brothers"
settings.when: the first of six sayings on the Law
settings.why: The commandment against murder (Exodus 20:13) binds every Israelite and was enforced by courts. Jesus applies it to the heart and the tongue, and gives two practical cases: make peace with a brother before worship, and settle with an opponent before court. The aim is a community without contempt.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, had no Temple after AD 70; they applied the altar saying to prayer and the Lord's Supper (Didache 14:2).

settings.to: all his hearers; the example is a man looking at a woman, since men held the legal power in marriage
settings.when: the second saying on the Law
settings.why: The command against adultery (Exodus 20:14) protected marriage, especially a man's rights over his wife. Jesus puts the burden on the man who looks with intent, and tells him to deal with himself, not to blame or hide the woman. The images of eye and hand are deliberate exaggeration.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, lived among Greek and Roman customs that allowed men far more sexual freedom than Jewish law did.

settings.to: the disciples, men in a society where only husbands could divorce
settings.when: the third saying on the Law; the debate returns in 19:3–12
settings.why: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulated divorce and required a certificate; the schools of Hillel and Shammai argued over the grounds. Jesus' answer protected wives, who could be sent away for little reason and left without support. By calling remarriage after such a divorce adultery, he denies that a certificate makes a wrongful divorce right.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, lived under Jewish rules that let a husband divorce for many reasons and Roman law that let either spouse divorce; they read the exception ("except for sexual sin") as their community's rule.
views: Matthew's exception allows a husband to divorce an unfaithful wife (most Protestants).
The exception refers to unions that were never lawful marriages (much Catholic teaching), or to betrothal (some scholars).
The exception allows a husband to separate from an unfaithful wife but not to marry again while she lives (Jerome, Augustine, Catholic teaching since Trent, some evangelicals).

settings.to: the disciples, and all who used oaths in daily business
settings.when: the fourth saying on the Law; compare 23:16–22
settings.why: The Law forbade false oaths by God's name (Leviticus 19:12) and required vows to be kept. In practice people swore by heaven, Jerusalem or their own heads to avoid God's name, and argued over which oaths counted. Jesus sweeps the system away: every word is spoken before God, so say yes or no and mean it.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, were asked to swear oaths in courts and in business, and in times of persecution to swear by the emperor; the passage shaped how they answered.

settings.to: the disciples and the crowds, ordinary people under Roman occupation and in debt
settings.when: the fifth saying on the Law
settings.why: "Eye for eye" set limits for judges. Jesus speaks to the person who has been wronged: the insulted, the sued, the conscripted, the borrower's neighbor. Instead of getting even, they are to answer with surprising generosity. For hearers who remembered the "fourth philosophy" of Judas the Galilean (AD 6), which taught that Israel should accept no master but God and resist Rome, the words had an edge.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, lived after the Jewish revolt of AD 66–70, which had ended in the Temple's destruction; Jesus' way of non-retaliation stood in contrast to that revolt.
views: The sayings forbid personal revenge; they do not address the state.
The sayings forbid all violence by Jesus' followers.
The sayings teach creative ways to resist injustice without violence (Wink).

settings.to: the disciples, who will face persecution (5:10–12)
settings.when: the last of the six sayings, the climax
settings.why: Leviticus 19:18 commanded love for the neighbor, usually understood as a fellow Israelite. Jesus extends love to the enemy and the persecutor and grounds it in God, who gives sun and rain to all. The goal is to be like the Father: whole, perfect, without limits in love.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, had real enemies: synagogue authorities who expelled them, Gentile neighbors who mocked them, Roman officials. They were told to pray for them.

traditions.q: Who is the Sermon on the Mount for, and can its commands really be obeyed?
views: The sermon is the "New Law" of the Gospel, the perfection of the old, given to all Christians and lived by the grace of the Holy Spirit (Catechism 1965–1970). Older Catholic theology distinguished commands binding on all from "counsels" of perfection followed by religious orders (Catechism 1973–1974); today the Church stresses that all are called to the fullness of holiness (Lumen Gentium 40).

The sermon is for Christians in their personal lives, not for rulers in their office. Luther taught that a Christian must suffer wrong for himself but may serve as judge or soldier for others. The sermon's demands also show everyone their sin and drive them to Christ.

Christ is not a new lawgiver but the true interpreter of the Law of Moses, clearing away false glosses (Calvin, Institutes 2.8.7). The sermon applies to all believers, who obey it imperfectly but truly by the Spirit.

The sermon is the rule of life for every believer, to be obeyed as it stands: no oaths, no use of the sword, love for enemies. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) based its rejection of oaths and the sword on Jesus' words here.

Classic dispensationalists, following the Scofield Reference Bible, taught that the sermon is the law of the coming kingdom: its primary application is to the future reign of Christ, though its moral principles teach the church today. Many later dispensationalists apply it more directly to Christians.

traditions.q: Does "not one iota ... will ever drop out of the Law" (5:18) mean the Law of Moses still binds Christians, and which parts?
views: The Old Law is holy but imperfect, a preparation fulfilled in Christ; its moral teaching, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binds. The Sabbath command is fulfilled in Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Catechism 1961–1964, 2175).

The ceremonial laws are ended and the civil laws expired with Israel's state, but the moral law, the Ten Commandments, binds everyone forever. The Sabbath is kept on the Lord's Day, Sunday, as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster Confession 19.3–5; 21.7).

The Ten Commandments are God's law for all, but the Sabbath command in its outward form, a particular day, was for the Jews; Christians keep it by hearing God's word, and gather on Sunday for good order (Large Catechism, Third Commandment).
Jesus did not abolish the Law. The Ten Commandments, including the seventh-day Sabbath, still bind Christians, and Saturday is the Sabbath to be kept holy (Fundamental Beliefs 19 and 20).

The Law of Moses was given to Israel as a whole system and was ended at the cross. Christians live under the law of Christ; nine of the Ten Commandments are repeated in the New Testament letters, but not the Sabbath.

traditions.q: Does the exception "except for sexual sin" (5:32) allow divorce, and may a divorced person remarry?
views: No exception allows remarriage. A valid sacramental marriage between baptized people, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power (Catechism 2382); separation may be allowed for grave reasons, including adultery (Catechism 2383), but remarriage while the spouse lives is adultery (Catechism 2384). The Council of Trent (Session 24, canon 7) taught that the bond is not dissolved even by adultery, following Jerome and Augustine, who read the exception as allowing separation only.

Marriage is meant to be lifelong, but the Church, by "economy" (pastoral mercy), may allow divorce for adultery and other grave causes and permit a second, even a third, marriage, celebrated with a more penitential service.
Divorce is allowed for adultery and for desertion, and the innocent party may remarry. Luther argued this in The Estate of Marriage (1522), reading 5:32 with 1 Corinthians 7:15.
Adultery after marriage, or desertion that cannot be remedied, gives the innocent party the right to divorce and to remarry as if the offending party were dead (Westminster Confession 24.5–6).

For centuries the Church of England taught that marriage is lifelong and did not remarry divorced people in church while a former spouse lived. Since 2002 its General Synod has allowed such marriages at a priest's discretion; Anglican provinces differ.

Divided. Baptists hold marriage to be a lifelong covenant (Baptist Faith and Message, article 18). Many allow divorce and remarriage for adultery or desertion; some allow no remarriage while the former spouse lives.

Historically very strict: the Amish and many conservative Mennonites allow no remarriage while a former spouse lives. Many Mennonite churches today allow it, with pastoral care (Mennonite Confession 1995, article 19, on marriage as a lifelong covenant).

traditions.q: Jesus says "do not take oaths at all" (5:34). May Christians swear an oath in court?
views: Jesus forbids rash and false oaths, not all oaths. Following Paul (2 Corinthians 1:23), an oath may be taken for grave and right reasons, such as in court (Catechism 2153–2155).
Christians may lawfully take oaths when the government requires them (Augsburg Confession, article 16). Jesus forbids swearing on one's own account, not oaths that serve truth and neighbor.
A lawful oath is a part of worship in which God is called to witness, and may be taken in weighty matters when required by lawful authority (Westminster Confession 22.1–3).

"Vain and rash swearing" is forbidden, but a Christian may swear when the magistrate requires it, in a matter of faith and charity (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 39). Methodist Articles of Religion keep the same article.
The Second London Confession teaches that lawful oaths may be taken when required by lawful authority, as in the Reformed confessions (chapter 23).
No. Christ forbids all swearing; believers' yes and no must suffice (Schleitheim Confession, article 7). Mennonites and Amish affirm instead of swearing.

No. Friends refused oaths from the start and suffered prison for it, arguing that Christ abolished all swearing; Robert Barclay defended this in his Apology (1676). Their stand helped win the legal right to affirm instead of swear.

traditions.q: "Do not set yourself against the evil person" (5:39). May Christians use force, as soldiers or police?
views: Legitimate defense is a right and, for those responsible for others, a duty (Catechism 2263–2265). War may be waged only under strict conditions of just war (Catechism 2309), and conscientious objectors should be provided for (Catechism 2311).

The Orthodox Church has no formal just-war doctrine. War may be a tragic necessity in defense of the innocent, but killing is never blessed: Basil the Great advised soldiers who killed in war to stay away from communion for three years (Letter 188, canon 13).

Christians may serve as rulers, judges and soldiers and may engage in just wars (Augsburg Confession, article 16). The sermon governs private life; the sword belongs to God's other kingdom, the state (Luther, Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved).
Christian magistrates may wage war on just and necessary occasions (Westminster Confession 23.2).
"It is lawful for Christian men, at the commandment of the Magistrate, to wear weapons, and serve in the wars" (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 37).
No. The sword is "outside the perfection of Christ"; believers do not use it (Schleitheim Confession, article 6). Mennonites, Brethren and Amish practice nonresistance and refuse military service.
No. The 1660 Declaration to Charles II states: "We utterly deny all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end, or under any pretence whatsoever."

traditions.q: "you are to be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (5:48). Can a Christian reach perfection in this life?
views: All Christians are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of love (Lumen Gentium 40, citing 5:48; Catechism 2013). Progress toward it is real, though perfection is completed only in heaven.
The goal of Christian life is theosis, sharing in God's life by grace; it is an endless growth that begins now and continues forever.

Yes, in a sense. Wesley taught "Christian perfection" or entire sanctification: a love for God and neighbor that rules the heart, possible in this life. It does not mean freedom from ignorance, mistakes or temptation (sermon Christian Perfection, 1741).

No. Sanctification is real but imperfect in this life; remnants of corruption remain in every part (Westminster Confession 13.2). Even the holiest have only a small beginning of perfect obedience (Heidelberg Catechism 114).

No. A Christian is at the same time righteous and a sinner (Luther, Lectures on Galatians, 1535; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 3). The command shows what God requires, and Christ's perfection is counted to the believer, who grows in holiness without reaching it here.
Divided. Holiness Pentecostal churches teach entire sanctification as a second work of grace, following Wesley; the Assemblies of God teach that sanctification is a lifelong process of growth.

title: For the Father Who Sees in Secret
sum: Jesus turns from the Law to the three great acts of Jewish devotion: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting (6:1–18). Each is to be done for God, not for an audience. The hypocrites who perform for people "are already paid in full"; the Father who sees what is hidden will repay those who act in secret. In the middle of this teaching Jesus gives his disciples a pattern for prayer, the Lord's Prayer (6:9–13), and stresses its line on forgiveness (6:14–15).

The second half is about money and worry (6:19–34). Treasure on earth decays; treasure in heaven lasts, and the heart follows the treasure. No one can serve both God and wealth. So the disciples are to stop worrying about food and clothes: the Father feeds the birds and dresses the lilies, and he knows what they need. They are to seek his kingdom and righteousness first and let tomorrow take care of itself.
readings: Read as a call to sincerity

The chapter attacks religion as performance. Giving, prayer and fasting are good, and Jesus assumes his followers will do all three ("when you give... when you pray... when you fast"), but they must be done for God's eyes only. On this reading the main word is "hidden."
Read as a call to trust

The chapter is about where security comes from. Reputation (6:1–18) and money (6:19–24) are false securities, and worry (6:25–34) is what life without trust feels like. On this reading the key is the word "Father," used twelve times in the chapter: disciples live as children of a Father who sees, knows and provides.

views.H: Almsgiving, prayer and fasting were the three pillars of Jewish piety in Jesus' time (Tobit 12:8 lists them together). Public prayer at set hours, fasts on Mondays and Thursdays by the devout (Didache 8:1 assumes this), and collections for the poor in synagogues are all well attested. No source mentions trumpets blown for donors; Jesus' picture is probably exaggeration. Galilean farmers knew well the worry about food and clothing, crop failure and debt.
views.C: The core of 6:1–18 (the three acts of devotion in parallel form) is found only in Matthew, and many scholars think Matthew inserted the Lord's Prayer into an older unit, since 6:7–15 breaks the pattern. Luke gives the prayer in a shorter form and another setting (Luke 11:2–4) and places the sayings on treasure and worry in Luke 12:22–34. Most think Luke's prayer is closer in length to the original and Matthew's closer in wording.
views.L: The chapter is built in two parts. 6:1 states the theme, and three matching paragraphs (6:2–4, 5–6, 16–18) each have the same shape: "when you...," do not be like the hypocrites, "Amen, I tell you, they are already paid in full," but you in secret, and "your Father, who sees what is hidden, will repay you." The Lord's Prayer sits at the center of the whole sermon. The second part moves through three contrasts (two treasures, two eyes, two masters) to the call not to worry, which ends with "seek first."
views.J: The Lord's Prayer is Jewish through and through. Its opening echoes the Kaddish ("May his great name be exalted and sanctified... may he establish his kingdom in your lifetime"), and its requests have parallels in the Eighteen Benedictions. Jewish teachers also warned against praying for show and taught that charity is best given in secret (Mishnah Shekalim 5:6 describes a "chamber of secrets" in the Temple for anonymous gifts). The "hypocrites" are a type found in every religion, not a description of all Pharisees.
views.T: The Lord's Prayer has been prayed in Christian worship since the earliest times: the Didache (about AD 100) tells believers to pray it three times a day. It is said at every Eucharist in nearly every tradition, and Tertullian called it "a summary of the whole gospel." The chapter's teaching on fasting shaped the church's fasts, and 6:16–18 is read on Ash Wednesday in the Western church. The call not to worry has been central to monastic poverty and to Christian teaching on providence.

deep.h: The Lord's Prayer: Matthew, Luke and the Didache
deep.b:
The prayer comes down in three early forms. Luke's is the shortest: "Father, may your name be honored as holy; may your kingdom come; give us each day our bread for the coming day; and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who owes us; and do not bring us into testing" (Luke 11:2–4, in the critical text). Matthew adds "Our... who is in heaven," "may your will be done," and "rescue us from the evil one." The Didache (8:2) gives Matthew's form almost word for word, with "debt" in the singular, and ends with "for yours is the power and the glory forever."

Many scholars think Luke has kept the original length and Matthew the original wording, and that the extra lines are liturgical expansions in Jewish style. Others think Jesus taught the prayer more than once in different forms. Either way, both are a pattern ("pray like this") as well as words to say.

The Greek word epiousios in 6:11 is found nowhere before the Gospels; Origen said the evangelists seem to have coined it (On Prayer 27.7). Four main meanings have been proposed:

  • For the coming day (from hē epiousa, "the next day"): bread for tomorrow, prayed for in the morning or the evening before. Jerome reports that the Gospel of the Hebrews read mahar, "tomorrow's." This translation follows that view.
  • Daily: bread for today, the meaning of the Old Latin cotidianum and of most English Bibles.
  • Needed for existence (from ousia, "being"): the bread we need to live. Chrysostom and many Greek fathers read it this way.
  • Supersubstantial: Jerome put supersubstantialem in Matthew in the Vulgate, which many Catholic and Orthodox writers have read as pointing to the Eucharist, the bread of heaven.

"The coming day" can also mean the age to come: on that reading the disciples ask for a share now in the bread of the kingdom feast. Those who take this view often point to Jesus' meals and to the Lord's Supper (26:29).

Most Protestant Christians end the prayer with "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen." The King James Version prints it in 6:13. The oldest Greek manuscripts of Matthew (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae), most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, and the early commentators Tertullian, Origen and Cyprian, who wrote whole works on the prayer, do not have it. Some early versions have shorter forms: the Old Latin Codex Bobiensis (k) has "for yours is the power forever and ever," and the Sahidic Coptic and the Didache (8:2) have "for yours is the power and the glory forever." Later manuscripts have longer forms. Most scholars think it was a liturgical response added in worship, following Jewish models such as 1 Chronicles 29:11, and then copied into the text. Catholics say it after the prayer at Mass, separated by a short prayer; the Orthodox priest sings it after the people say the prayer. See the variant on 6:13.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the prayer answers the three "hypocrite" scenes
deep.b: The Lord's Prayer sits inside a passage on doing piety for God's eyes. Its first three requests (name, kingdom, will) move the one praying from self-display to God's honor, which is exactly what the hypocrites lack (6:2, 5, 16). Its last three (bread, forgiveness, rescue) match the second half of the chapter: bread answers the worry about food (6:25–34), forgiveness of debts answers the pull of wealth and treasure (6:19–24), and rescue from the evil one answers the eye that is "evil" (6:23). If this is right, Matthew placed the prayer as a hinge: it gathers what comes before and opens what comes after. This is my reading of the arrangement; commentators note the prayer's central place, but I have not seen this exact pairing proposed.

echoes: Luke 11:1–4; Luke 12:22–34; Luke 16:13; Tobit 4:7–11; Tobit 12:8; Isaiah 58:3–9; 1 Chronicles 29:11; Exodus 16:4; Ezekiel 36:23; Psalm 147:9; Job 38:41; 1 Kings 10:4–7; Proverbs 27:1; 26:39; 26:41; James 4:13–14; 1 Timothy 6:6–10

settings.what: Teaching on giving, prayer and fasting
settings.to: the disciples, devout Jews who already gave alms, prayed at set times and fasted
settings.when: the middle of the sermon, after the teaching on the Law
settings.why: In a village or town everyone could see who gave, who prayed at the street corner, who looked pale from fasting. Religious standing brought honor. Jesus tells his disciples to take their piety out of that market of honor: the only audience that matters is the Father, who sees in secret.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, kept these practices but set themselves apart from the synagogue: the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, "not with the hypocrites," and to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day (Didache 8).

settings.by: Jesus, teaching a pattern of prayer
settings.to: the disciples, as a group ("Our Father," "give us")
settings.when: in Matthew, within the sermon; in Luke, when a disciple asks, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1)
settings.why: Teachers often gave their followers a short prayer that marked them as a group, as John the Baptist did. Jesus' prayer is brief, in contrast to the many words of 6:7, and it teaches disciples to put God's honor and kingdom first and then to ask for what they need for the day, for forgiveness and for protection.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, prayed it together in worship, probably in Aramaic or Greek, as the prayer that marked them as Jesus' people.
views: Jesus gave words to be repeated, as the church has done ever since (Luke 11:2, "When you pray, say").
"Pray like this" gives a model for the shape of all prayer; some Puritans and Quakers did not repeat it as a set form.

settings.to: the disciples, many of whom had left their work to follow him (4:18–22), and poor listeners in the crowds
settings.when: after the teaching on secret devotion
settings.why: For people who lived close to hunger, worry about food and clothing was constant, and wealth seemed the only security. Jesus tells them that the Father who feeds the birds knows their needs, and that chasing wealth makes it a master. The call is to trust, not to stop working: birds do not sow, but they still hunt for food.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, included both poor members and some with property; the passage spoke to both, as 19:16–30 does.

traditions.q: Should Christians pray the Lord's Prayer word for word, and does "forgive us our debts" (6:12) apply to believers already forgiven?
views: The Lord's Prayer is "the summary of the whole gospel" and the most perfect of prayers (Catechism 2761, 2774, quoting Tertullian and Aquinas). It is prayed at every Mass and in the rosary. The baptized ask daily for forgiveness of the sins they still commit (Catechism 2838–2845).

The Our Father is prayed at every Divine Liturgy just before Communion, and many times in the daily prayers. The petition for forgiveness is a daily confession, and the request for bread is often read as a request for the Eucharist.

Luther's Small Catechism explains each petition. On the fifth he says that Christians sin daily and deserve nothing but punishment, so they pray that God would not look on their sins, and they promise in turn to forgive.

The prayer is a pattern for all prayer and may also be used as a prayer (Westminster Shorter Catechism 99–107). The Heidelberg Catechism 126 explains "forgive us our debts" as a plea for Christ's blood not to count our sins against us.
Early Friends did not use set prayers in worship, including the Lord's Prayer, since prayer should come only as the Spirit moves; they treated the prayer as a pattern.

The Scofield Reference Bible noted that 6:12 asks forgiveness on the condition of forgiving, which it called "legal ground," and contrasted it with Ephesians 4:32, where believers forgive because God has forgiven them. Many dispensationalists still pray the prayer but read it as a model, not a church liturgy.

traditions.q: Jesus says "when you fast" (6:16) and that his followers will fast once the bridegroom is taken away (9:15). Should churches keep set fast days?
views: Yes. Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting, and Fridays are days of penance; the Church sets these to unite believers in penitence (Catechism 2043; Code of Canon Law 1249–1253).

Yes, very much so. Most Wednesdays and Fridays are fast days, along with four longer fasts each year (Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast, the Dormition Fast and the Nativity Fast), when meat, dairy, and often fish, wine and oil are not eaten.
Fasting is a good outward training, but church rules about foods and days must not be imposed as necessary for salvation (Augsburg Confession, article 26). Many Lutherans observe Lent voluntarily.
The Book of Common Prayer lists days of fasting and abstinence (the forty days of Lent, Ember Days, Fridays), though how strictly they are kept varies widely.
Fasting is right on special occasions, called by the church in times of trouble or need (Westminster Confession 21.5), but not set by a church calendar.
Fasting is a private spiritual discipline, practiced freely by individuals or called by a congregation "upon special occasions" (Second London Confession 22.5); there are no set fast days.

title: The Narrow Gate and the House on Rock
sum: Jesus warns against judging others while blind to one's own faults: first pull the beam from your own eye (7:1–5). Holy things must not be given to dogs (7:6). He urges his disciples to keep asking, looking and knocking, because the Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask, more than any human father would (7:7–11). Then comes the summary of the whole teaching on the Law: "whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them" (7:12).

The sermon ends with warnings, each a pair: two gates and two roads (7:13–14), good and rotten trees, a test for false prophets (7:15–20), those who say "Lord, Lord" and those who do the Father's will (7:21–23), and two builders, one on rock and one on sand (7:24–27). Hearing is not enough; the one who acts on Jesus' words will stand. The crowds are astounded, because he teaches with an authority of his own (7:28–29).
readings: Read as the call to decide

The chapter, especially 7:13–27, turns the sermon into a choice. Every listener stands at a fork: the narrow gate or the wide one, the rock or the sand. On this reading the sermon is not a set of ideals to admire but a demand to act now.
Read as wisdom for community life

The first half (7:1–12) is about how disciples treat each other: no judging, discerning what is holy, asking God for good things, the Golden Rule. On this reading the chapter sketches a community marked by humility and generosity, warned against false leaders from within.

views.H: The pictures are from village life: a carpenter's beam and splinter, bread and fish as daily food, wolves and sheep, thorns and thistles, houses built in a land of sudden winter floods. Builders in Galilee did dig down to rock when they could; a wadi bed looked like a fine level site in summer and became a torrent in winter. The ending, "he taught with authority," fits the impression Jesus left on many (Mark 1:22).
views.C: Most of the chapter has parallels in Luke 6 and 11 and so is usually assigned to the source Matthew shares with Luke. Matthew has shaped the warnings into a series of pairs. Many critical scholars think the false prophets of 7:15–23 were a problem in Matthew's own church (compare 24:11, 24), probably charismatic leaders who did not keep the Law ("lawlessness," 7:23).
views.L: The Golden Rule (7:12) closes the body of the sermon that began at 5:17 with "the Law or the Prophets." The ending follows the pattern of covenant speeches, which end with blessings and curses and a call to choose (Deuteronomy 30:15–20; compare the two ways in Psalm 1). Matthew's closing line (7:28) is repeated, with small changes, at the end of every one of his five discourses (11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).
views.J: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn it" is the famous answer of Hillel, a generation before Jesus (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Tobit 4:15 has the same rule in negative form. The "two ways" are a deep Jewish theme (Deuteronomy 30; Psalm 1; Jeremiah 21:8), and "with what measure you measure" is a rabbinic principle (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). Jesus speaks as Jewish teachers did, but the crowds note that he did not cite authorities.
views.T: The Golden Rule became one of the best-known sayings of Jesus; John Wesley and many others treated it as the heart of Christian ethics, and the name "Golden Rule" goes back to the 1600s. "Judge not" has been quoted widely, often against any moral judgment, though the passage goes on to require discernment (7:6, 15–20). The parable of the two builders is a favorite in children's teaching. Many traditions have read 7:21–23 as a warning against claiming faith or spiritual gifts without obedience.

deep.h: The Golden Rule in other traditions
deep.b:
The rule of treating others as one would be treated is found across the ancient world, mostly in negative form:

  • Tobit 4:15 (about 200 BC): "Do not do to anyone what you hate."
  • Hillel (about 10 BC): "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor" (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a).
  • Confucius (about 500 BC): "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others" (Analects 15.24).
  • Seneca (about AD 60): give as you would wish to receive (On Benefits 2.1.1).

Christian writers have often argued that Jesus' positive form asks more: it requires doing good, not only avoiding harm. Jewish scholars have answered that Hillel's negative form is not weaker, since it goes with "go and learn" the whole Torah, and that Leviticus 19:18 already commands positive love. Jesus' version links the rule to "the Law and the Prophets," as Hillel did to "the whole Torah," and to the Father's generosity in 7:7–11, which comes just before.

Scholars disagree about the sermon's outline, but many see this frame:

  • Introduction (5:3–16): the blessings and the call to be salt and light.
  • The Law and the Prophets (5:17–20) opens the main body.
  • Greater righteousness toward the Law (5:21–48): six sayings.
  • Greater righteousness toward God (6:1–18): giving, prayer, fasting, with the Lord's Prayer at the center.
  • Greater righteousness in daily life (6:19–7:11): money, worry, judging, asking.
  • "That is the Law and the Prophets" (7:12) closes the main body.
  • Conclusion (7:13–27): warnings in pairs.

Dale Allison has argued that much of the sermon is built in threes (1987); Günther Bornkamm proposed that 6:19–7:12 follows the Lord's Prayer petition by petition (1978), and Robert Guelich and Ulrich Luz took up his proposal. Neither proposal has won general agreement, but both show how carefully the sermon is arranged.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the "fool" thread
deep.b: Matthew uses the Greek root mōr-, "foolish, dull," three times in the sermon, and each comes at a turning point. In 5:13 salt that "goes flat" is literally salt that "becomes foolish" (mōranthē). In 5:22 calling a brother "You idiot!" (mōre) brings the fire of Gehenna. In 7:26 the man who builds on sand is "foolish" (mōros). Read together, they suggest a frame: disciples who lose their saltiness become "fools" in God's sense, the very word they must never throw at a brother, and the true fool is the one who hears and does not do. Matthew's later parable of the foolish and sensible bridesmaids (25:1–13) uses the same pair of words as 7:24–26. Scholars have noticed the wordplay in 5:13 and the link of 7:24–26 with 25:1–13; the three-point frame is my suggestion.

echoes: Luke 6:31; Luke 6:37–49; Luke 11:9–13; Luke 13:23–27; Tobit 4:15; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 30:15–20; Psalm 1; Psalm 6:8; Jeremiah 21:8; Ezekiel 13:10–16; Proverbs 10:25; 3:10; 12:33; 24:11; 24:24; 25:1–13; 25:12; Romans 2:1; Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14; James 1:22–25; James 2:14–26

settings.what: Judging, asking, and the Golden Rule
settings.to: the disciples, as members of a community of "brothers"
settings.when: near the end of the sermon's main body
settings.why: Small groups that take holiness seriously are quick to judge each other. Jesus forbids the harsh, hypocritical judging that ignores one's own faults, while still requiring wisdom about what is holy (7:6). Then he points the disciples to the Father, who gives good gifts, and sums up how they must treat others.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, had their own rules for correcting a brother who sinned (18:15–17); 7:1–5 set the spirit in which those rules were to be used.

settings.to: the disciples and the listening crowds, who have heard the whole sermon
settings.when: at the end of the sermon
settings.why: Like Moses at the end of Deuteronomy, Jesus sets before his hearers a choice between life and ruin. The warnings address the danger of hearing without doing, of following false prophets, and of trusting in spiritual experiences without obedience. The point of the whole sermon is that it be lived.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, faced prophets and leaders in their own churches whose lives did not match their words (24:11, 24); 7:15–23 gave them a test: watch the fruit.
views: The false prophets are outside teachers, such as Jewish leaders or Zealot prophets.
Most scholars think they are Christian prophets within Matthew's churches, since they call Jesus "Lord" and work miracles in his name.

settings.what: The parable of the two builders
settings.to: everyone who has heard the sermon, disciples and crowds alike ("anyone who listens to these words of mine")
settings.when: the last words of the sermon
settings.why: Galilean hearers knew houses of mud brick and stone, and dry stream beds that looked like good level ground until the winter rains turned them into torrents. The point is not the builder's skill but his foundation: hearing Jesus without doing what he says is building on sand. The storm stands for the testing of life and for God's final judgment.
settings.readers: Matthew's first readers, most likely Jewish followers of Jesus in Syria or Galilee in the decades after the Temple fell in AD 70, had seen a city and its Temple fall; the parable told them which house would stand.
views: The flood is the last judgment, as in the prophets' storm pictures (Ezekiel 13:10–16).
The storm is any crisis that tests a life, now as well as at the end.

traditions.q: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs" (7:6). Should communion be open to all who come, or closed to those outside the church?
views: Communion is given only to Orthodox Christians who have prepared by prayer, fasting and confession. The Didache (9:5) already quotes 7:6 about the Eucharist: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs." The deacon's call before the Creed, "The doors! The doors!," once closed the church to the unbaptized.

Holy Communion is for Catholics in a state of grace; other Christians may receive only in special cases, with Eastern Orthodox Christians more freely admitted than Protestants (Catechism 1385, 1398–1401).

Divided. Confessional Lutherans such as the Missouri Synod practice close communion, admitting those who share their confession of the Real Presence. Many Lutheran churches, such as the ELCA, welcome all baptized Christians.
The table is "fenced": ignorant and openly ungodly people may not come (Westminster Confession 29.8). Most Reformed churches welcome baptized believers from other churches who profess faith.

The table is open: all who love Christ, repent of their sin and seek to live in peace with one another are invited. Wesley called the Supper a "converting ordinance" that can bring people to faith (Journal, June 1740); the United Methodist statement This Holy Mystery (2004) affirms the open table.
Divided. Many Baptists practice open communion for all believers; some practice close communion, limited to those baptized as believers, and some only for members of the local church.
